en: Re-30577 Determination of Impurity (āśaucanirṇayaḥ) (p.
Salutation to that venerable Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the cataract of ignorance was opened with the medicinal probe of the collyrium of knowledge. (L. 2) [Accompanied] by Guha.
A *yuga*, two *yugas*, three *yugas*, and four *yugas* [are the periods];
then, in order, there are the Caṇḍāla, the *sūtaka*, and the *udakyā*. ... [Whatever is] otherwise acquired by oneself, whether through friendship or marriage, is not shared with the heirs.
Having prostrated before the Lotus-eyed One, the crest-jewel of gods and demons, who is served by Brahmā, Rudra, and others, I shall set forth the determination of impurity (*āśauca-nirṇaya*).
Salutations to the emperor of the Vaidikas, the illustrious Nārāyaṇa Paṭṭa Śrī. (l.

2) Having paid homage, [the author] explains, by means of the Śolliki Rōma, the cause that renders one impure prior to the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and other rites during the period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*).

"When it is stated that 'impurity lasts until the bath at the [proper] time,' [this refers to the following: (l.3) for the sake of purification, one must perform the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), sesame, water, and so forth; however, there is no power to perform such rites for a deceased person who has been cremated. Therefore, the bath is prescribed. (l.4)

Whatever remains as that which is called *āśauca* (impurity), it is stated: "In both the case of death (*śāva*) and birth (*sūta*), the abandonment of ritual acts is prescribed; even the ritual materials become defiled, and Vedic study is forbidden. Thus, in both the impurity caused by a corpse (*śavāśauca*) and the impurity caused by childbirth (*sūtaka*), all ritual acts are to be abandoned.
They defile even the ritual substances;

they prohibit even the study of the Vedas. Therefore, regarding the rites for the deceased, one should cause the performance of the *sādhya* karma, the *agnihotra*, and the *śrāddha* by someone other than an Ārya; one should not perform these oneself.

This means that one must perform the *saṃdhyāvandana* and the funeral rites (*pretakārya*) after bathing; likewise, one must perform the *agnihotra* by carrying the fire elsewhere and leave it there, and one must not give [the fire] away.

In times of distress (*āpad*), that which is to be accepted as a gift may always be given by the master; it may also be taken by others there for the sake of increasing the mother’s prosperity. In times of distress, one must not refuse a gift, nor should one be ashamed to ask for it. This is the domain of the man who employs means for his livelihood: curd, milk, ghee, vegetables, pungent spices, flowers, sesame, medicinal herbs, wood, roots, fruits, meat, honey, well-water, and clothing.

One may take [these items] oneself with the permission of the owner. Even during a period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*), curd, milk, honey, salt, flowers, grain, medicine, land, fruits, uncultivated forest produce (*uñchana*), water from the southern bank [of a river], a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), and all such final [items] may be accepted; there is no fault in taking these even when the patron (*yajamāna*) is present.

The sage has accepted that one may accept cooked food prepared by a cook, as well as various kinds of edibles, whether cooked or uncooked, such as rice and the like; however, these must be obtained from the house of one who is a regular giver of food. If the sacrificer is a person who habitually gives food, one may take fruits and rice from his house.

Because it is meritorious, the birth of a son is to be accepted as such by others; thus, on the day of the son's birth, one may perform the *tilodaka* offering. This too should be understood [as auspicious]. Regarding the impurity (*āśauca*) for one who eats the funeral food (*aghāhāra*), the learned say that it lasts for a day and a night, ending with the moonrise. Just as milk mixed with ghee [remains] until it is digested, so too the impurity falls away once the food has been consumed and digested. If one eats intentionally while residing in a house of impurity, one remains in that state of impurity.
(From page 7b, line 1:
While [observing] the *candrāyaṇa* vow,
if one eats food unknowingly, there shall be impurity (*āśauca*) lasting from the time it is digested until it passes through the lower orifice.

An impurity (*āpad*) caused by death (*jñāti*) results in fault for one who eats at his own home; however, if he eats [elsewhere], there is no fault for the *jñātis*. Whatever impurity belongs to the husband, that much pertains to the wife; the wife does not possess the impurity of the husband. If the husband has an impurity due to death, it applies to the women as well; the impurity of the women does not apply to the husband. Regarding the impurity of the mother and other [relatives] of the women, the husband also undergoes that same impurity.

Impurity resulting from contact (*samparkāśauca*) lasts for the duration of those days. For women, there is no impurity regarding their property or ritual activities; such impurity belongs only to the [male] relatives. Regarding impurity through contact: instruction in the rites for the deceased (*pretakarma*), performing those rites together with others, living together, eating in the same row (*sapaṅkti*), and traveling together—these they declare to be *sampat*.

Even if one performs the funeral rites (*pretakriyā*) for kinsmen, or performs the funeral rites oneself for a *vichāla* (an outcaste), or shares a meal with someone due to the impurity of birth (*sūtaka*), that is *samparkāśauca* (impurity through contact). When a priest (*ṛtvij*) or others perform a *homa*, a *śrāddha*, or other rites at any time, they should do so wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*); for the performer, it should be over the right shoulder (*apāsavya*).
In cases of *samparkāśauca*, the performer remains under the influence of that impurity until the end of the period.

In the context where it is stated that there is no impurity (*āśauca*) for ritual acts (*kriyā*), when one performs the *śrāddha* rite by treating it as having been obtained through a lapse of time (*prāptakāla*), the performer (*kartṛ*) must wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) [for the ancestors], while the one performing the rite must wear it over the left shoulder (*upavītī*). Likewise, regarding the materials for new rites (*navakriyā*), the period of three days and so forth has passed; thus, even when the impurity (*āśauca*) has elapsed, there is no impurity regarding the materials for the rites.

It applies to women as well. One should perform the *jīvaśrāddha* for oneself during the ten-day period; for others, there is no impurity (*agha*). Regarding the *jīvaśrāddha*: one must observe the mother’s period of impurity (*mātṛmāśauca*) for oneself; there is no [impurity] for relatives (*jñāti*) and the like. Until the end of the period of death-impurity (*āntaśāve*), one should avoid touch; in the case of birth-impurity (*sūti*), [one should avoid touch] for four days. For the impurity of touch (*sparśanāgha*), bathing is prescribed; for one who is impure (*āśaucin*), penances (*kṛcchra*) are ordained. In the case of death-impurity (*mṛtāśūtaka*), one may not be touched until the end of the ten days. In the case of birth-impurity (*jananasūtaka*)...

The *nūla* and *nūl* [periods] cannot be touched. For those who have not undergone the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), touching [such a person] requires only a bath (*snāna*). If one touches someone affected by the impurity of another birth-impurity (*anyasūtaka*), there is a penance (*prāyaścitta*).
It is stated that during the period of birth-impurity (*janana*), the *nūla* and *nūl* may be touched; however, this refers specifically to the *Kṛtayuga*.
[There is also] the village funeral rite (*grāmapretapūjā*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*).

When a corpse or a *caṇḍāla* is present in a village, for Brahmins and others in particular, one must never study, eat, or converse [with them]. (l. 6) One should perform the *homa* and other rites in a pure village that is free of corpses; one should do so at a distance of eleven *dhanus* from the edge of the village. When there is a conflict between the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti*, the *Śruti* alone is more authoritative. Therefore, one should offer the *śrauta* oblation even within a village containing a corpse. (l. 7) Thus it is said. Within the village, even when a corpse is present, the *smārta* rites and the daily *homa* [may be performed]. (l. 8)

Śiva-pūjā and Vedic study are not permitted. The Agnihotra may be performed, but the Paśubandha and similar sacrifices are to be avoided. Because there are eleven other castes [to be excluded] and because they belong to the Nārāśa division, all ritual acts (*sakala-karmāṇi*) may be performed. When there are thirty [houses], it is called a *palli*; up to a hundred, it is called a *grāma*; and up to a thousand, it is to be known as a *raṅga*.

And [the impurity lasts] until the boundary markers and the outskirts of the village; that region shall become impure. In a village containing four hundred Brahmins, the individual rites for a corpse must be performed.
If there is a woman, a Śūdra, or an outcaste, or likewise others such as a young child or the sun...
(l. 3) ...if a corpse is present in the middle of the village, all the rites may be performed. [This applies even if there is] a woman, a Śūdra, or an outcaste. (l. 4)

Regarding the death of a child or an *arka* [tree], some sages maintain that rituals should not be performed; this is one view (*pakṣa*). In the case of death during the course of a ritual of worship (*pūjāvidhi*), one should complete the remainder of the rite according to the *tantra* alone. However, if death occurs outside the village after the conclusion of the ritual, one should carry out the funeral rites for the deceased according to the prescribed rules. If death occurs in the midst of the worship, one should perform the remainder of the rite according to the *tantra*, and thereafter carry out the funeral rites for the corpse according to the injunctions. [The same applies] to the birth of a daughter... [etc.]

In the case of a daughter’s birth or death, there is impurity (*aśauca*) for three generations; for males, it extends to seven generations, but not so for the two [the father and mother] regarding the *piṇḍa* offering. At the birth of a daughter, as well as at death, there is impurity for three generations. This threefold sequence is as follows: at the birth of a daughter, the brother, the father, his brother, and his son, and the grandfather and his brother, become pure after ten days.

[Impurity] other than that arising from marriage [is determined by] the purity at the time of taking [the bride]; for three days in the case of a maiden's menses, and full [impurity] in the event of death among kinsmen. Āpastamba says: "In the case of an immature maiden, immediate purification is ordained. An immature maiden is one who has not yet undergone the *caula* ceremony, but after the time of the first cutting of hair (*kṣura-kāla*). Upon the death of a maiden, there is impurity for one day. Up until the time of the *vādāna* ceremony, there is impurity; after the *vādāna*, there is a three-day impurity for both parties. Even if there is no formal gift (*dāna*), if it extends to seven persons, there is a three-day impurity for the kinsmen.

This is because it serves as an indicator for the time of the word "giving" (*dāna*). In the case of the death of a maiden, there is impurity (*āśauca*) lasting ten days for both parents and brothers. Even if she has not been "mounted" (*arūḍha*)—that is, even if she dies after the occurrence of menstruation prior to marriage—there is the impurity prescribed for her own caste for the paternal family. The term "the deceased" (*mṛtaḥ*) refers to the father-in-law, the brothers, the father, the paternal uncles, and their children.

For that [person], for his brothers, and for their wives, there is impurity (*āśauca*) for ten days. If a boy (*piḷḷai*) is born, there is impurity until the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). This is *jananāśauca* (impurity due to birth). (l. 7) Regarding *śiśumaraṇāśauca* (impurity due to the death of an infant): there is a distinction in the case of the death of a child (*bāla*). From birth until the *cūḍākaraṇa* (tonsure), it is traditionally held that impurity lasts one night; from the performance of the first feeding (*prāśana*) until the initiation (*upanayana*), it lasts three nights; and after that, it lasts ten nights. [This applies] to those other than the father and brothers. (l. 8)

In the case of the death of a child among kinsmen (*jñāti*), there is purification by mere bathing for those aged three years and older. For those under three years of age, until the *caula* ceremony, there is impurity for only one day. After the *caula* and until the *upanayana*, there is impurity for three days. After the *upanayana*, there is full impurity. Until the *cūḍā* ceremony, there is immediate purification; this applies to women as well.

For those who have died an unnatural death, however, the relatives become pure after three days. Even in the case of Brahmans, if a girl dies anywhere from birth until the end of the *caula* ceremony, there shall always be immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) for all castes.

From that point until the completion of the *vākya-kṛta-dāna* (the rite of giving her away), it is indeed one day; beyond that, when she has reached marriageable age, the certainty is three nights. Thus it is said. [Regarding] a girl born... up to three years...

For maternal uncles (*mariścāl*), there is merely bathing (*snānamātram*) for three years; beyond that, up until the age of seven, there is one day of impurity (*ekāhāśauca*). From the eighth year until marriage (*pāṇigrahaṇa*), there is three days of impurity. And for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras... [the rule of] impurity [is as follows].

For the castes, the periods of impurity (*āśauca*) due to birth or death are ten, sixteen, twenty, and thirty nights respectively; this is the consensus of many sages. For Brahmins, there is ten days of impurity during birth and death; for Kṣatriyas, eighteen days; for Vaiśyas, one month; and for Śūdras, there is a period of three months of impurity. The impurity for the primary performer [of the rites] lasts until the release of the deceased.

Even for sons, there is impurity (*āśauca*) until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony, even if they are the ones who performed the cremation (*mukhakartṛ*). After that, they are unfit for their own duties regarding rites for the gods and ancestors. Furthermore, disciples, slaves, brothers, and kinsmen (*bhrātṛka*) [are affected] by the impurity arising from the death of one’s own *piṇḍa* [relative]. If those residing in the same household [are affected], then the teacher, the master, and others are likewise subject to impurity.

For disciples and servants, there is impurity (*āśauca*) due to their own kin; for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, they must observe the impurity of their own Guru for one month. For Vaiṣṇava Śūdras, female slaves, and [female] attendants, the duration is half a month. (l.

2) For Śākta, Ātma-vaiṣṇavas, Śūdra female slaves, and Śūdra male slaves—if they conduct themselves according to the rules of conduct (*ācāra-niyama*)—there is fifteen days of impurity due to their kin. [This applies to] those who are joined with women. (l. 3)

And those married to men of a different caste become pure at the time of the husband's [death]. Their sons, upon his death, become pure according to the period prescribed for the maternal relatives. If a Brāhmaṇa marries the daughters of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, (l. 4) those women have the impurity (*āśauca*) of ten days following that of their husband. For their children, in the event of the father's death, there is impurity for eleven days for the sons of Kṣatriya women, (l. 5) twenty days for the sons of Vaiśya women, and thirty days for the sons of Śūdra women.

Impurity according to seniority (*kramāśauca*) and impurity according to merit (*guṇāśauca*). It should not be performed; it should not be performed. In the Kali age, the contraction of the period of impurity (*aghasaṅkocana*) [is forbidden]; impurity by seniority and impurity by merit must be discarded from afar in the Kali age. As stated in the *Kaviyukti*: "Impurity by seniority and impurities by merit must be avoided. Impurity (*āśauca*) is as follows: "In the fourth [generation], there shall be ten nights; for a man, six and a half [nights] in the fifth."

"In the sixth [case], purification occurs after four days; in the seventh, however, after three days. Thus it is said. For the *jñāti* [agnates] and *sapiṇḍas*, the sequence is ten days; for the *anta-sānta* [distant relatives], nine days; for the *āraruṇṭala* [more distant], eight days; and for the *eṇāntala* [even more distant], seven days—this is known as *krama-āśauca* (sequential impurity).
One should also understand *guṇa-āśauca* (qualitative impurity): "In one day, one is purified... [and so on].

A Brāhmaṇa who possesses the three Vedas [remains impure] for three days; one who possesses only the Vedas [remains so] for ten days, provided he is devoid of virtuous qualities. For one who is destitute of ritual action, for a miser, likewise for one burdened by debt, and for a hypocrite, the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) lasts until the reduction to ashes [of the body]. A "miser" (*kadarya*) is one who harms his father and mother. Thus it is said that in the case of the death of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), there is impurity for one day.

For one who knows only the Vedas (*kevalavedin*), there is impurity (*āśauca*) for three days; for one who does not study the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), there is impurity for ten days. Furthermore, for those who have abandoned the deceased (*pretabhraṣṭa*), the mute (*mūka*), those who harm their mother or father (*mātṛpitṛhimsaka*), those burdened by debt (*ṛṇagrasta*), and the hypocritical (*ḍāmbhika*), there is impurity until the cremation. Regarding that which is called "purity through merit" (*guṇaśauca*), both of these [types of purity] are to be avoided during the Kali age.

The domain of "flowing" (*srāva*) and "falling" (*pāta*). For the father, it is indeed "flowing" (*srava*) and so forth; for others, it is "falling" (*patana*) and so forth. Among those beginning with "flowing"—in the case of relatives, there is bathing (*snāna*) upon the "falling. Up to the fourth month is "flowing" (*srāva*); in the fifth and sixth months, it is "falling" (*pāta*). Until the end of nine months it is "flowing"; in the fifth and sixth [months] it is "falling."

In the case of a *pāda* [impurity], it is prescribed as immediate for kinsmen (*jñāti*), while for paternal ancestors (*pitṛ-ādi*) and others, it is remembered as lasting three days. In the case of a *kaṭhina-pāta*, it lasts for three days. (p. 11a, l. 1) As for a fall (*pāta*) [of impurity] affecting the mother, it lasts for one month; for paternal ancestors and others, it is three days. In the case of a *pāda* [fall], it lasts for five months for the mother. (Verse 5) For six months, it lasts for six days; for the father, it lasts for the same number of days [as the months]. (l. 2)
This concerns the subject of those who have died or been born.

Whether it be one born after death or one dead after being born, according to the teaching of Hārīta, the full period of impurity for kinsmen lasts ten days following the occurrence. Even if the placenta falls out, or even if it does not fall out—for kinsmen, there is full impurity for ten days. In the case of a miscarriage during the first three months, the impurity lasts for three days; beyond that, the impurity lasts for a number of days equal to the number of months elapsed. After six months, however, the impurity lasts for the remaining period until delivery.

The Procedure for Childbirth (Sūtikā-vidhi): For the mother, there is impurity for three days during the first three months; from the fourth month up to the sixth month, it is according to the number of months in days; from the seventh month onwards—at whatever time it may be, whether within the month or after it—there is full impurity (pūrṇāśauca). This applies likewise to the father and the paternal kinsmen (jñātis).

In the case of a woman giving birth to a daughter, there shall be forty days of impurity for the mother; in the case of a son, thirty days. For a relative (*jñāti*), it is ten days in both cases. If a daughter is born, the mother is not fit for ritual activities for forty days; if a son is born, she is unfit for forty days. There is a period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasting ten days for both the mother and father, as well as for their relatives.

One should avoid seeing or speaking with a woman who has recently given birth for ten days; thereafter, she may see others, but she herself must not be seen by them. For ten days, she is considered impure (*asuci*) and unfit for religious rites (*kukkava*). (l. 2) Regarding the father of a newborn, there is contact-impurity (*sparśa-aśauca*) until the end of the period of defilement (*aghāntam*). This applies even when a daughter is born. There is no additional period of impurity. In the case of the birth of a maiden, the same rule applies to brothers born of different mothers (*bhinnodara*). (l. 3)

It is not desired [that impurity] apply to the son of a brother. There is impurity (*āśauca*) for brothers-in-law; there is no such thing as the absence of it for nephews—this is the alternative view (*pakṣa*). (l.

4) By the previous statement, "at birth and death," the rule of ten days (*daśāha*) for kinsmen (*jñāti*) was already stated. Nevertheless, because both women and men may have sons of half-brothers and so forth, this is stated again—without distinction between those born of different wombs—to confirm the Smṛti texts that full impurity (*sūtaka*) applies to all *sapiṇḍas*, whether female or male. [This concerns] the kinsman (*jñāti*). (l. 6)

The singular number here is intended to refer to the class [of relatives]. For three nights thereafter, there is impurity for paternal and maternal kinsmen (*jñāti*) upon the death of a daughter or a son; and for a full period [of ten days] in the case of a brother or parents, always when a daughter or a young child dies. Regarding the death of a daughter who has been given away or one who is unmarried: for the paternal kinsmen and the [maternal] kinsmen, there is impurity for three days; for the mother, father, and brothers, it is ten [days].

It exists every day. Even in the case of the death of a maiden or a child, this same [impurity] increases; there is full impurity (*pūrṇāśauca*). "Whether the sacraments such as naming (*nāma*) and so forth have been performed at the prescribed time, or whether they have not been performed at all, or whether they were performed out of their proper time—if a person dies, the impurity (*agha*) is exactly the same in these cases. Just as if the sacraments such as naming were performed at the proper time—or even if they were not performed due to the lapse of the proper time—whatever the case may be, one must accept it accordingly. After the *caula* ceremony, cremation (*dāha*) occurs; before the naming ceremony, burial (*khanana*) occurs. Or rather, cremation or burial [is determined by the stage of life].

"Or rather, [the rite] for one who has lost his teeth. This means that cremation is established as occurring after the *caula* ceremony; however, if death occurs before the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), one should perform burial (*khanana*). If death occurs after the naming ceremony but before the eruption of teeth, one may perform either cremation or burial. For one whose teeth have erupted, one may perform the ritual of renunciation (*tyāga*). This is based on the performance of the rites (*karmaṭa-nibandhana*). [Verse: "If a son is born who has not yet emerged from the womb, for all the *sapiṇḍas* there shall be a great impurity (*maha-magha*). For one whose teeth have not yet appeared, [the period of impurity lasts] for months... (l. 7)

"Or if death occurs within six months, or within five months, or within three months, or if a child dies before reaching two years of age, immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) is prescribed. No water-libation (*udaka-kriyā*) should be performed by relatives for a child less than three years old"—because of such statements, the duration of impurity is determined by the passage of time. This is what [the text] says. If death occurs within six months from birth, even if the funeral rites are not performed, there is one day of impurity for the *jñātis* (agnates).

This refers to a male [deceased]; this also is based on time. By the term "eruption of teeth," the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) itself is intended. Furthermore, the scriptural statement: "One should bury a deceased child less than two years old, but not offer water; having followed him as far as the cemetery, the other kinsmen, observing their vows, should return"—this refers to a case where the timing is fixed. If one performs the tonsure (*caula*) at the age of three years and four months, burial (*khanana*) is prescribed. Beyond that, cremation (*dahana*) is the rule. In the case of cremation, the impurity lasts for one day; in the case of burial, it is immediate; and beyond the eruption of teeth, in the case of burial, it lasts for three days.

In the case of abandoning the body [by burial], a three-day impurity is prescribed. For those who abandon [the child] through cremation, there is one day of impurity for the relatives (*jñāti*s). Regarding burial, it is merely abandonment; it should be performed on the first, third, or seventh day, according to the injunction of the *Śruti*: "Like a young sprout," and so forth. Because of such scriptural injunctions, from the time of naming until before the eruption of teeth, there is only bathing for the relatives after burial. In the case of cremation, there is one day of impurity. The ritual water-offering (*udakakriyā*) should not be performed by relatives for a child under three years of age; however, one may perform it for a child whose teeth have erupted, or even for one whose naming has occurred, provided the sequence is observed.

Prior to three years [of age], one should perform *tarpaṇa* for the relatives (*jñāti*). If cremation (*dahana*) is performed, one must perform *tarpaṇa* only for the father; in the case of burial (*khanana*), there is no *tarpaṇa*. For a child beyond three years, water [libations] are offered seventy-five times. After three nights, ten *piṇḍas* are given, and *tarpaṇa* shall be performed for all; this applies to unmarried girls, boys, and those who died prematurely.

"One should perform the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and the water-libation (*udakakriyā*) for three days; the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for ten days—of this there is no doubt. This refers to the death of a girl or a child within the first three years. In such cases, the father must perform both the monetary offering (*arbudha-paṇa*) and the rice-ball offering for ten days. If others perform these rites, they must complete them all within three days and observe the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for ten days. This rule applies until the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).

"Until three years have passed, there shall be water and rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for three days; from the eighth year onwards, the offering of rice-balls shall continue for ten days. When the wife of the deceased is abandoned or when an infant is buried, then, starting from that very day, the rule of immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is prescribed. Thus it is said. From birth until before the time of initiation (*upanayana*), if death occurs, there is impurity (*āśauca*) after the burial; in the case of cremation, there is impurity after the cremation.

Even in the case of renunciation (*tyāga*), there is impurity (*āśauca*) thereafter; bathing is required for one day, six days, or three days, according to these rules. Regarding birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), it lasts for ten nights starting from the day of death. After the *caula* ceremony, there shall be a three-night period; after the observance of vows (*vrata*), that is, after the *caula*, there is a three-day period for relatives. After the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*), [the period is as follows].

The ten-night period (*daśarātra*). If deaths occur during the third part of a three-watch night, it is considered an impurity (*aghama*) starting from the following morning; if they occur within the first two parts, it is considered an impurity starting from the preceding watch. Having divided the night—excluding the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*)—into three parts, if [the death] occurs in the third part, it belongs to the following day; if it occurs in the seventh part, it belongs to the middle day... this is [the rule].

It is the same [regarding the period of impurity] for both the birth and the death [of a child], as well as during the seasons. For one who performs sacrifices (*yajvan*), the impurity regarding the sin of the day of death and so forth lasts for ten days starting from the cremation; for one who does not perform sacrifices (*ayajvan*), however, it lasts for ten days starting from the cremation itself. If there is a doubt as to whether one is a sacrificer or not, [the rule is: for those who perform sacrifices, the period begins from the cremation and lasts until the end of the third fortnight (*traipakṣika*); for those who do not perform sacrifices, it begins from the death and lasts for ten days. Beyond that, whatever *śrāddha* is performed on the anniversary of the day of death, it should be conducted according to the lunar date (*tithi*). However, in the case of a twice-born (*dvijaman*) who maintains the sacred fire (*kuhitāgni*), the cremation should be performed first. For those who perform sacrifices, the period begins from the cremation and extends up to the end of the third fortnight.

Now, regarding death and cremation, starting from the *tithi* [lunar day] and so forth: "In the case of impurity due to death, there is twelve days' impurity for the kinsmen (*jñātis*) solely because of the death, and likewise for the cremator because of the cremation.

Since it is stated here that "for the kinsmen solely because of the death," this refers to those other than the cremator who is distinct from the son or the kinsman; [it applies] even in the case of the cremation of a sacrificer (*yajvan*). Thus, it is said: "for the kinsmen, [impurity begins] from death and so forth. This is intended to exclude the cremator who is not a son or a kinsman.

If the re-burning (*punardāha*) of either a sacrificer (*yajvan*) or a non-sacrificer (*ayajvan*) occurs within ten days, the impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for three days; however, if it occurs before the completion of the [initial] period of impurity, the full [ten-day] period applies. (l. 3) Regarding the re-burning of both a sacrificer and a non-sacrificer, if it takes place within the ten-day period, the impurity lasts for three days. (l.

4) If it occurs after ten nights have passed, there is impurity for ten nights starting from the day of death, provided it is not performed by a son or others. In the case of the re-burning of a non-sacrificer... (l. 5)

Regarding kinsmen (*jñāti*), even if [the deceased] was not a performer of sacrifices (*ayajvā*), there is impurity (*āśauca*) for ten days; likewise, even if he was a performer of sacrifices (*yajvā*), there is impurity for ten days. Furthermore, if the *asthi-saṃskāra* (bone-rite) has not been performed within ten days, there is impurity for ten days for all kinsmen as well. This is one view (*pakṣa*). Regarding the burning of bones: "In the case of burning the natural [bones], it is prescribed that [impurity lasts] three days; however, in the case of burning a substitute [image], it is desired that [impurity lasts] ten nights for the *sapiṇḍas* and the sons, whether they are performers of sacrifices or non-performers. This is another view.

Regarding the impurity (*āśauca*) for the cremation of bones with *darbha* grass: if it occurs on the eleventh day, it lasts for three days for the *jñātis*, but for sons, it lasts for ten days; this is the view of the *ṛṣis*. Furthermore, this refers to the domain of the *Gautama* [tradition]. "There is no sin in performing it again if it was previously undertaken. Manu has declared that there is impurity for those who offer the water libations (*udaka-dāna*) in this case. For *jñātis* who were previously present, it lasts for ten days. However, for one who performs the cremation of the bones himself, or performs the re-cremation (*punardahana*), there is no impurity for the *jñātis*.

If one is the *putrakartṛ* (the performer of the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* on behalf of a son), there is impurity (*āśauca*) for ten days from the first day. Furthermore, if he is the *itarakartṛ* (another performer), then until the previous day has passed, he must not perform the *mukhya-śrāddha*, nor the *pañcāhnika-śrāddha*, nor the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.

The meaning of the statement regarding the "taking of the *piṇḍa*" as the occasion (*nimitta*) will be explained later. For those who are *mukhakartṛ*s, [the rites] such as cremation (*daha*) and so forth [apply].

The occasion [of impurity] lasts until the end of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite; for kinsmen (*jñāti*), the occasion is merely the offering of water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*); for relatives (*bandhu*), the occasion is merely bathing. All of these are set aside by time as well as by bathing. Furthermore, the village impurity caused by that corpse, as well as the birth impurity for kinsmen other than paternal uncles (*pitṛvya*)—[these too are set aside].

All the sesame-water offerings (*tilaudaka*) are poured out by his kinsmen; however, the offering of the garment-water (*vāsodaka*) and the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is prescribed for the performer alone. While all such acts as the offering of garment-water and the rice-ball are duties of the performer, the sesame-water is merely for the kinsmen. Upon hearing of the death of one's parents while they are absent, [the impurity lasts] ten nights; [if heard] after three days—

"However, for the wife of a brother, it lasts ten days; after a year, ten days. This means: if the death of a mother or father occurs while one is in another country (*deśāntara*) and the news reaches within ten nights, the impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for ten nights. Even if it reaches after that, for those other than the son, it begins from the day the news arrives and lasts for ten days. If a sister-in-law dies and the news reaches within one year, it lasts ten days; if it reaches after a year, it lasts three days. As it is said: "If the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) have been performed, [the impurity] lasts for three days at the end of the year for those two."

The general rule is that for those who have performed the funeral rites (*uttarakriyā*) for their parents, it lasts one year; for sons, three days; and for younger brothers, one day. Regarding the case where the father has died while away on a journey and the son has gone to another country: "If the rites have been performed, [the impurity] shall last three nights; if the rites have not been performed, it shall last ten days. Even when the father's rites have been performed, the prescription of three days is indeed the rule for the younger brother. Thus, "if the rites have been performed, it is three nights" is the statement.

Even regarding the case of a younger brother who has gone to another country, it is said: "In the event of the death of a brother living abroad, the performance of the *piṇḍa* and *udaka* rites [is required]; there, the period of impurity (*sūtaka*) lasts for three nights, but for the wife and son, it lasts for ten days. This refers to the intention that the funeral rites (*pretakṛtya*) are to be performed by the surviving relatives even after ten days. For brothers, however, the impurity lasts for three days. Regarding the death of a brother in a foreign land: "If [the death occurs] within six months or less than a year... (l. 3).

For one who has performed the cremation of a brother who died in a foreign land, there shall be a ten-day period; however, if it is more than six months but within a year, it shall be three days. For the one who performs the cremation, it is ten days—this is the statement of Vaiṭhīnasi. But for one whose *udaka* (water-libation) rites have been performed, a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night) is desired if it is within six months; if it is beyond that, three days should be observed. If the rites have not been performed, it is ten days. This applies to the death of a brother in a foreign land regarding the performance of the ritual.

If death occurs within six months [of birth], there is impurity for three days; if it occurs after that, there is impurity for one day for the year. If a bird dies, and no funeral rites (*kriyā*) are performed, it is said that there is impurity for ten days (*daśāha*). (l. 7) This is the view of Gālava. All of this is not accepted by Vijñāneśvara and others. "But when ten days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights; if three months have passed... (l. 8)

Because it is established by the statement of Manu and others that "it should be for three nights," and because even that Smṛti which protects the meaning of Manu perishes [if contradicted], and because it is censured as being in conflict with the Smṛtis of Manu and others; furthermore, because of the absence of such practice—[this view] is not to be accepted. For among all people, only those who are learned (*śiṣṭa*) are recognized as authorities; if [the practice] were lost within ten nights, [the authority would vanish].

Impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for nine days [for those other than sons] prior to the collection of the bones (*sañcayana*). It is traditionally held that until the collection of the bones, the impurity lasts for nine days; thereafter, it is ten nights. For sons, however, if the collection of the bones is performed before the tenth day, the impurity lasts for nine days. From the third day onwards, and from the day of death until the tenth day, there is impurity. Even if the collection of the bones is performed on the eleventh day or earlier, after that—

There is impurity for ten days starting from the day of death. When a son hears of the death of his father or mother while within the ten-day period, his purification shall occur after ten days from the date of death, provided he performs the funeral rites (pretakārya).

One should understand that any śrāddha performed for the deceased—such as the *navaśrāddha* and others—is as if not done at all, unless the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is performed. If a son hears of the death of his mother or father during the ten days of impurity, his purification occurs after ten nights starting from the day of death. On the eleventh day, he must perform the *ekoddiṣṭa*. [The *ekoddiṣṭa* must be performed...]

...if [the period of impurity] has passed, one may perform the *samasta* (comprehensive) *tīrtha-parva*. Even if one is impure, one should perform the *ādya-śrāddha* on the eleventh day; for the performer, there is immediate purity (*tātkālikī-śuddhi*), though he remains otherwise impure.
As it is said:
"The *śrāddha* which is ordained to be performed on the eleventh day from death... If the eldest son (*jyeṣṭha*) arrives during the ten-day period and performs the rites (*kriyā*), [then...]

Even if there is impurity (*āśauca*) for ten days, if one remains impure until the sixteenth day from the day of death, one may still perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, because that period is pure for that purpose. If the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed by either the eldest or the youngest son, how should it be for sons who have gone to another land?

Upon hearing [of the death], they should perform shaving and offer water with sesame seeds for ten days; thereafter, they should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the eleventh day. Śātātapa stated that one should perform it on the twelfth day.

"If both parents have died while residing in another country, even another [relative] may perform the entire ancestral rites (*paitṛka*). However, excluding the cremation, the eldest son must also perform everything, including the *sapiṇḍana* with the younger brothers. Thus it is said. After the younger brother has performed the *sapiṇḍikaraṇa*, the elder brother should undergo the shaving of his head starting from the day of death (*kedānāl*) and observe the period of impurity (*sūtaka*) for ten days. During those ten days, he should offer only water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*). On the sixteenth day, the *sapiṇḍikaraṇa* is performed.

One may perform the *piṇḍa* offering even without the word "preta. However, if the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has not been completed, one must wait until the tenth day from the date of death. On that tenth day, having first undergone a haircut (*kṣaura*), one may perform only the *tilodaka* (water with sesame seeds) offering. If the primary performer of the rites is unavailable, even one who is otherwise qualified may abandon the ritual duties [only if necessary].

Then the performer of the rite (*saṃskartṛ*) should perform the [funeral] acts and release [the body] from there. Furthermore, one should perform all the rites, including the offering of water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*), the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), the covering of the naked, and the presentation of the nine *śrāddhas*.

(Verse 4) This should be understood as referring to the primary performer who arrives during the ten-day period. [Note: If the primary performer is someone other than the mother or father, he should not remain under the control of the son while the rites are being performed. Even that son, until the cremation, [should remain under his authority] starting from the first day.

The offering of sesame-water and rice-balls (*tilodakapiṇḍadāna*), the covering of the naked, the *navaśrāddha*, and all such rites must be performed day by day. (l. 7) Even for one who has completed the funeral rites (*kṛtakriya*), if he performs the *pitṛkārya* [on the tenth day], he remains in a state of impurity (*sūtakī*) for ten days. He should offer sesame-water to his son, and again perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite.
If one residing in a foreign land hears [the news] from time to time, he should offer water with sesame seeds; however, he should avoid the offering of *piṇḍas*.

By the word *piṇḍa*, the *navaśrāddha*, the *ekottaravṛddhi*, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, and so forth are included. There is no bathing on a mountain, nor the offering of a *pretapiṇḍa*, nor the *ekottaravṛddhi* [śrāddha]. He should not offer a handful of water with a cloth. Until the tenth day, every day, he should offer water with sesame seeds upon a clump of *darbha* grass. This applies to the performer of the *mukha* [śrāddha] at that time or during the interval of ten days.

If [the deceased] dies after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has already been performed, one should offer only *tilodaka* (water with sesame seeds) starting from the day of death until the completion of the *ṣaḍardha-nārāyaṇa-śānti*. Then, one must perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* again. Not a single rite, such as the offering of the *piṇḍas* or the *navāśrāddhas*, shall be omitted; furthermore, the installation of the *śilā* (foundation stone) and the term *preta* (the departed spirit) shall cease. Moreover: "When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been completed, if a son hears of the death of his parents, he should offer [the rites] here, beginning from that day, for ten days."

If, after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, one should utter the word *preta*, he becomes a violator of the sacred law (*vidhighna*) and is born as a slayer of his ancestors (*pitṛghātaka*). Therefore, after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*,

when offering water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*), the primary performer and all the kinsmen should abandon the word *preta* and instead use the expression "O [Name], belonging to the [Gotra] lineage."

One must offer water with *darbha* grass upon the great ground. By the single word "preta," one attains great liberation (*mahāmokṣa*). Having produced the *preta*, performed the consecration (*saṃskāra*), and taught him the Veda, the father—should that [father] have perished, he should provide a livelihood for twelve days for the great teacher (*mahāguru*). If the father himself performs the *jātakarman* and other *saṃskāras*, and teaches him the study of the Vedas and all the secret doctrines (*rahasya*), he is called the "great teacher. Upon his death...

For sons, there is impurity for twelve days. Until the end of the twelfth day, one should not perform the worship of deities, nor should one perform ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*), as well as fire-offerings (*homa*) and recitations (*japa*). On the thirteenth day after a death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), on the eleventh day after a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), during an eclipse on the following day, and on the fifth day after menstruation—until the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is completed, the performer of the funeral rites attains purification through the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water, as well as by the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). Impurity due to death (*śāvam āśauca*) lasts for ten days.

It is ordained regarding sapinda relatives: for the performer of the funeral rites (*saṃskartṛ*), the performance of divine and ancestral rites, as well as *japa*, *homa*, and so forth, must be avoided for a period of twelve days. In the case of death-impurity (*mṛta-sūtaka*), purification occurs on the day following [the end of the period] for the performer of the rites. There is also one view that purification lasts until the completion of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. After the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), there is purification.

In the case of birth, purification occurs on the eleventh day; in the case of the day of an eclipse, purification occurs on the same day; and in the case of the onset of menses, purification occurs on the fourth day. In both types of impurity (*aśauca*), for all kinsmen, purification is on the eleventh day. For three months [of pregnancy], it is three nights (*trirātra*);

after that, for three [months], it is a *pakṣiṇī* [period]; thereafter, for six months, it is a *svadhā* [period]; and upon hearing of death after ten nights, there is purification by bathing. Thus, the impurity of death lasts ten days for all, and for three months [of pregnancy]...

Impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for three days; the libation (*tarpaṇa*) lasts for three days. From four months up to six months, there is impurity for one *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night). From seven months up to a year, there is impurity for one day. If the child dies after a year, there is only bathing and libation, and no birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the son and other relatives perform the libation; the term "preta" is dropped, as is the placing of the water-pot (*kuṇḍa*) and the offering of water with cloth (*vāsodaka*). In cases of extreme impurity, there is one day [of purification] for those who are otherwise purified by three days or ten days.
In the case of those for whom the period of impurity (*sūtaka*) lasts ten days, three days, or one day, if [the news] reaches them after that time has elapsed, there is purification after one day.

Regarding *pakṣiṇī* (two days with an intervening night): if it reaches after two full days have passed, there is purification after one day. If it reaches after the first day has passed, there is purification after one day; if it reaches after the second day has passed, there is purification after one day; if it reaches during the intervening night, there is purification after that night alone. Thus, for one whose [period of impurity] lasts one day, it is one day.

From the death of a second-degree relative (*reṇḍānāl*) up to a seventh-degree relative (*keṭṭāl*), there is merely bathing (*snānamātram*). For others beyond that, there is no impurity for one who has not yet been initiated (*anupeta*). Regarding the lapse of purification (*atikrāntaśauca*) for an uninitiated person, it applies to his mother and father;

(l. 4) it also applies to his brother and his stepmother, as well as to their sons, but not to other kinsmen (*jñāti*). This refers to the case of death in a foreign land (*deśāntaramaraṇa*). There is bathing for the father, but not for the others, nor does that [impurity] persist after the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) has passed. (l. 5)

Impurity due to birth lasts ten days for the father; for him, it is merely a bath. For *jñātis* (agnates), there is no bath. If, during that period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), there occurs the death of that same son or another death, (l.

6) if the secondary factor (*aṅga*) has already been declared by the former [rule], there is never impurity from death (*śāva*) distinct from the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). If, in the midst of birth-impurity, another birth-impurity occurs, (l. 7) the subsequent birth-impurity applies to the *jñātis*. It also generally applies to the performer of the funeral rites (*kartṛ*). If, in the midst of impurity due to death, another death-impurity occurs, (l. 8) [the same rule applies].

Even if birth-impurity (*jananāśauca*) occurs during a previous period of impurity, it does not apply to sons; rather, one must observe ten nights (*daśarātra*). If death-impurity (*maraṇāśauca*) occurs within the midst of birth-impurity, one must observe three nights (*trirātra*). If a three-night period of impurity occurs in the middle of that initial [period], one becomes pure at the end of the former [period].

After that impurity due to death (*maraṇāśauca*), one becomes pure; [however,] if a birth-impurity (*jananāśauca*) occurs in the midst of it—[that is,] if a child dies while [the mother is still] within [the period of] postpartum impurity—the prior death-impurity prevails. (l. 3) In some places, this very meaning is expressed by the word "kvacit" (in some cases): "But if the death of one born [during] the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) occurs, for the father, two days are prescribed until the end of that [period]; at dawn, it shall be three days. If it occurs on the day following the first [period], it is likewise; from the end of the prior [period], it is two days, and after that, three days; or if it occurs in the final watch of the prior [period], it is at dawn. (l. 4–5)

In the case of a prior period of impurity (*pūrvāśauca*), if a ten-day period of impurity (*punardaśāhāśauca*) occurs, there shall be a three-day period of impurity for the mother. (l. 6) If it occurs during the night, it ceases before sunrise; thereafter, there shall be a three-day period. If it occurs after sunrise, it lasts until the end of that ten-day period. (l.

7) "When two periods of impurity meet, one should discard the shorter in favor of the longer, not the longer in favor of the shorter. For the shorter is removed by the arrival of another day at dawn or otherwise."
Thus it is said:

if a *tryaha* (three-day) impurity or similar occurs during a *daśāha* (ten-day) birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), one becomes pure according to the preceding [period]. If a *daśāha* birth-impurity occurs during a *tryaha* or similar impurity, the former [period] continues. Even if the rites for the tenth day are lost, one remains impure for the remainder of the longer period. If there is death among the paternal kin, or if there is death while the mother is still in her period of impurity (*mātṛāśauca*), [the following applies].

Or [in the case] of the father: if the death of the father occurs within ten days [of an initial impurity], there shall be a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night) after that impurity. If the death of the mother or father occurs during the period of impurity for a relative (*jñāti*), there is a ten-day period starting from the day of death. If the death of the mother occurs during the period of the father’s death, there is a *pakṣiṇī* after the ten days of the father. If the death of the father occurs during the period of the mother’s death, there is a ten-night period starting from the day of that death. On the first day of the mother’s [impurity], for them—

Having performed the *ekāha* rite on the eleventh day for the father, one should also perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the twelfth day. For the mother, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed during the third fortnight (*traipakṣika*).
For others, the funeral rites (*pretakāryāṇi*) should be performed upon the death of a *mahāguru*, and the *śrāddha* should be offered before the completion of one year.

But one should avoid [the following]: "One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the *śrāddha* together with the monthly offerings (*māsika*) within the year," according to this statement. Furthermore, according to the statement: "When the wife, son, daughter-in-law, grandson, brother, his sons, and both parents are to be honored in a single year, one should perform the first [offering] on the eleventh day, but the *sapiṇḍana* after three fortnights. If the performer acts within ten days [of death], [then...]

Furthermore, for the deceased, there is the re-consecration (*saṃskṛti*); therefore, purification results from the remainder of the previous [rite]. The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is declared by Vasiṣṭha; it is prescribed on the eleventh day at midday. (l. 4) If there are two acts of cremation, they belong specifically to the performer [of the rites] according to their order. Even so, this second *piṇḍa* must always be offered according to the former [procedure]. (l. 5) If the one who performs the cremation carries out the burning of the corpse within ten days, purification shall occur through the former [rite]; for the parents, however, it shall take place from that day. This is according to the rule for a single performer. (l. 6)

"If many funeral rites for the deceased are to be performed, there may be purification according to the time [of each rite], yet he remains impure once again"—so it is said. If one performs another consecration (*saṃskāra*) between the mother’s and father’s [funeral rites], one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* on his first anniversary day and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* at the end of the year. [And] one's own wife and son...

The grandson (*pautra*), the brother, and his son—if these have undergone the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) during the interim period—one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for each on the eleventh day and perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* during their respective three-fortnightly periods (*tripakṣa*). If, however, one person undergoes the sacramental rites after another has already passed through the ten-day period of impurity (*daśāha*) due to the death of a mother or father, he becomes pure immediately following that prior period of impurity. For each such person, one should perform the *ekāha* rite on the eleventh day and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* during the three-fortnightly period.

In the case of two persons [dying] within ten days of each other, the *saṃskāra* (funeral rites) shall be performed first for the one who died earlier; for the other person, the period of impurity (*daśāha*) lasts for ten days. After performing the offerings of sesame water, rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), and so forth, the *ekādaśāha-śrāddha* (the eleventh-day rite) for each shall be performed on their respective eleventh day, and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on their respective fourteenth day. For the one who died earlier, purification occurs at the end of the ten-day period. In the case of multiple cremations, after the performer has performed the rites for immediate purification (*kālikāśuddhi*), he remains impure until the previous day [of the next scheduled rite].

(p.21b, l.1) ...that [is] a hundred [of offerings]. There shall be purification together with the husband, and the *śrāddha* shall take place on a single day. Whether it be the mother-in-law or the mother, (l.2) having performed all the rites beginning from the day of death (*mṛtadivasa*) of the father up to the *ekoddiṣṭa*, [one should perform them] for the father. (l.3)

On the day of the *ekoddiṣṭa* for the mother, one must perform an *ekoddiṣṭa* for each [mother]. On both the first and middle days, one must perform only the *sapiṇḍana*. If the wife has passed away before her husband, the son shall perform the *ekānviti*, the *nirmalya*, and the *daśāhahoma-śravaṇa*; he shall perform the *piṇḍa*, *udaka*, and other rites separately. Having bathed, having offered the *śaktikoda* [libation], and having fanned [the funeral pyre] with the breath of swords, he, with a clear mind, [should address] his husband who has ascended the funeral pyre praised as new: "O you who have crossed over... (bhūyantāri).

The son should lay his mother to rest with a mantra, or he may cremate her after [the husband], but not before the bath together with the husband. Regarding the practice of *anumaraṇa* (following the husband in death): for one who has performed the funeral rites for his father and all other [ancestors]—having caused the mother to lie down [on the pyre] amidst the [funeral] fires—after that, she should take her bath.

Having performed the giving of gifts according to one's capacity (yathā-śakti-dāna), having provided her with a cool breeze (sigvāta), and having caused her to offer salutations—with the mantra beginning "This woman [goes] to the world of her husband"—the mother should cause her to lie down upon a bed made of *śitāpī* grass. Immediately thereafter, the consecrations (saṃskāras) and other rites must be performed. Herein is the specific detail.

The gold fragment (*hiraṇyaśakala*), the cloth for covering the naked (*nagnaprachādana*), the stone slab (*śilā*), the sesame-water offering (*tilodaka*), the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), the nine *śrāddhas* increasing by one each time, the water-pot (*udakumbha*), and the release of the bull (*vṛṣotsarga*)—these sixteen [rites] must each be performed individually. The preparation of the sacrificial porridge (*carukārya*), the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), the collection of bones (*sañcayana*), and the propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*)—these are to be performed only once. When a woman follows her deceased husband on the following day, her *śrāddha* should be performed on the anniversary of his death according to the prescribed rule. Her husband has indeed departed [from this world].

Even if one performs *anumarana* (self-immolation following the husband), the rites for the husband are completed in a single day (*ekāha*). However, as an extension of that, if there is a difference in the lunar day (*tithibheda*), one should perform [the rites] for two days according to the *tantra* system.

The sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) for the couple is performed together, whether the wife dies first or follows the husband in death. All the funeral rites (*pretakāryāṇi*), beginning with the offering of water (*udaka*) and ending with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, are likewise performed together.

One should perform the *sāmvatsarika* (annual) rite as well as the three [other rites] completed together. Here, the Smṛti texts record that the *sāmvatsarika* depends upon the mental resolve (*manana*). Even if the husband and wife die on different lunar days (*tithi*), if they have performed *anumaraṇa* (following in death), one should perform everything from the water-offering (*udaka*) up to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* in a single day, and may also perform the annual rites (*pratyābdika*) together.

Regarding the different lunar days (*tithi*), the monthly rites (*māsika*) and so forth, as well as the annual rites (*pratyābdika*), should be performed according to the specific *tithi*. As it is said: "In the case of birth and death, in sexual intercourse, in brushing the teeth, and in oil massage, the *tithi* at which one bathes with curd is declared to be effective for that entire day (*kālikī*). On whichever day a person dies, marked by a particular month, fortnight, and *tithi*, the annual rite for him on that same day is called the *kṣayāha* (the anniversary of the passing)."

The wise know that [these acts] are joined with the lunar day (tithi) associated with the specific time—whether at birth or death, during sexual union, or while cleaning the teeth. Regarding the lunar day belonging to the month and fortnight:

"When the Śrāddha for a son has arrived, whether it be fresh or even stale, the son should perform it beginning with the ancestors (pitṛs), unless there is an engagement with another [obligation]. [This applies] to the mother as well.

Regarding the annual rites (*pratyābdika*): at the time of performing the annual rite on a single lunar day (*tithi*), one should perform it as a single portion, dividing it for both the father and the mother, even if they died at different times. Even if they were other [relatives], it is generally performed on a single *tithi*. When there is sufficient capacity, one may perform them separately. In the case of the simultaneous death of a husband and wife, however, the cremation and other rites should always be performed together. Prior to the cremation and until the destruction [of the body], they are treated as one; but after that, the rites are separate. Likewise, the son’s *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for the mother should be performed together with that for the father.

The rite should be performed together with the eldest [son]; it may be separate only for the sake of a specific occasion (*nimitta*). When the rite is being performed on account of such an occasion, what purpose is served by the *preta* [offerings] alone? These include: the *cakṣuṣka*, the *kṛṣṇa-śāmalaka*, the *japya*, the *prāñjali*, the *piṇḍadāna*, the *sodakumbha-śrāddha*, the *ekottara-vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the *ekāha-sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the sixteen *śrāddhas*, the *vṛṣotsarga*, and so forth; these bring satisfaction to the *preta*. For the *preta-homa*, one *piṇḍa*, the meal, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and so on, must each be performed separately. Herein lies the benefit.

The meaning is that in the second pit (*kuṇḍa*), the *śāntihoma*, the cooked food offering (*pāka*), the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, the selection of officiants (*varaṇa*), and so forth, must be performed. Here, [the rites] from the *ekoddiṣṭa* and *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* onwards... [p.23b, l.1] ...the *pāka*, the *vaiśvadeva*, and the *ādikahoma* constitute the common procedure (*tantra*). Here, by the term *ekoddiṣṭa*, the monthly rites (*māsika*) are meant; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the annual anniversary rite (*pratyābdika*) is included. (l.2)

By the term *vaiśvadeva* and others, the selection of the ancestors (*pitṛ-varaṇa*) is indicated. This means that during the simultaneous performance of the rites for both parents at one time, all the obligatory rites (*nitya-kriyā*) must be performed up until the cremation; however, after the cremation, everything pertaining to the deceased (*preta-nimitta*) must be performed individually. What are these items pertaining to the deceased? They are: silent recitation (*japa*), the offering of water (*śila*), the offering of sesame-water and funeral cakes (*tilodaka-piṇḍa-pradāna*), the water-jar (*sodakumbha*), the increasing by one [offering] each day (*ekottara-vṛddhi*), the single-day rite (*ekāha*), the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the sixteenth [rite], the release of the bull (*vṛṣotsarga*), and the *preta-homa*.

The *arghya*, the *piṇḍa*, the feeding of Brahmins, and the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)—all these should be performed individually. The funeral pyre (*citikuṇḍa*), the *śāntihoma*, the cooked offering (*pāka*), and the selection of Viṣṇu among the Vaiśvadeva and Pitṛs—these too must be performed individually. Regarding the *pākahoma*, there is one offering to the Viśvedevas and Viṣṇu; this is how it should be done for the monthly and annual rites. Then, on a single day, the cooking for both mother and father is prepared together; first the rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkarmāṇi*), and secondly [the rites for the mother].

The same applies to the mother. There should be a single *agnaukaraṇa* offering, and the *arghya* water should be offered separately for each. Three *piṇḍas* are prescribed for both the father and the mother.

For both together, there is a single *saṃkalpa*, a single sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and separate stones [for the hearths]. This means that even if the mother and father pass away on the same lunar day, the portioning and the selection of Viṣṇu for the *vaiśvadeva* rite [are performed separately].

The *homa* [is performed]. One [offering] for the father and mother; one for the paternal grandfather and grandmother; [and] the *kriyās*. The *arghya* with pure water, three times for each. One should offer three *piṇḍas* for each. The *saṃkalpa*: (l.

4) "On this auspicious fifth lunar day, for the two ancestors, the deceased father and mother, belonging to the [such-and-such] *gotra*, named Parameśvara-śarman and Pārvatī, in this *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa-śrāddha*—or in an *ekoddiṣṭa-śrāddha* or an annual *pratyābdika-śrāddha*—thus one should perform the *saṃkalpa*. (l. 5–6) If the wife follows her deceased husband and enters the blazing fire..."

In that case, one should observe a *pakṣiṇī* [period of impurity] for the paternal ancestors; O God, one becomes pure after that. In the event of following the deceased in death (*anumaraṇa*), after ten days have passed, the mother and the others must observe a *pakṣiṇī*. From the time of their own period of impurity... [the relatives] shall be purified through the conjunction with merit (*aghayoga*), while the father is purified by the remainder of the previous period of impurity. Even in the midst of the period of impurity for a relative... [they are purified].

[This applies] even to one who has performed the *saṃskāra* [of cremation]. For these three types of persons, the *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth) follows from the preceding *āśauca* (impurity). If one has cremated several ancestors (*pitr-nyanantara*) in succession, he becomes pure by the end of the period of the first [impurity]. If he should cremate both his father and mother, the one who performs the cremation becomes pure after ten days. If there should be two acts of cremation, the performer becomes pure by the same rule without distinction; however, for the parents, purity occurs on that very day. If [the second cremation] occurs within the ten-day period of the performer—

Furthermore, there is the consecration (*saṃskṛti*) of the deceased; from that, purification follows as a remainder of the previous [period]. The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is performed according to the prescribed time. This means that even if another impurity (*saṃkarī*) occurs during the ten-day period for one's mother or father, one must perform the *piṇḍa-bali* offerings at their respective times, provided they have not already been performed. Likewise, if the death of one's own mother or father occurs during the ten-day period of another [impurity]— [Note: The text fragment ends here.]

From the day of death until the end of the ten-day period, one must perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for each respective person on each respective day. For those other than the wife and so forth—for all others—one must perform the *sapiṇḍana* at the end of the year for the mother and father; for others, it may or may not be performed. If the annual (*ābdika*) rite for others has already been performed [prior to that], [the procedure is as follows].

Even before that [time], one may perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Even if the mother, wife, and others die within the year following the father’s death, their *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed during the third fortnight (*trai-pakṣika*) after their respective deaths. This refers to cases where the same person performs the rites for all. Regarding the text: "In the case of a birth occurring during a period of impurity (*sūtaka*), the learned prescribe a remainder of eight days; but for the father, two days; on the third day, it becomes pure. By the word "but" (*tu*), the rule regarding *śāva* (impurity due to death) is excluded from the rule regarding *sūtaka* in certain instances. This negates the previously stated meaning. If a child born during a period of *sūtaka* dies, the remaining eight days of impurity apply to the *sapiṇḍas* caused by the birth.

Sin arises from both birth and death; upon the birth or death of an infant, there is always impurity for the parents because of their state of being completely filled with impurity (*pūrṇāśucitva*). On the final day of the *sūtaka* period, if that [infant] dies, there is further impurity for two days beyond that. At dawn, it becomes three days. For the mother, it should be exactly thus; however, the word "known" (*jñāta*) indicates that which lasts for two or three days. By the mention of "father and mother," brothers are excluded. Regarding "by one who has performed the naming ceremony, for uterine siblings," this is the rule for ten days. This refers to the rule of ten days.

[This is] because of the prescription of impurity due to death for brothers [in the rule]: "The rule regarding death-impurity for brothers... It means: if [a death occurs] during the period of birth-impurity (*jananasūtaka*), that birth-impurity (*janmatta*) shall apply to those who have become [afflicted by it]. For those who die, there is indeed both birth-impurity and death-impurity for the mother and father, as well as for the *jñātis* (agnates). Those *prajas* (l. 2)...

In the case of a death occurring on the tenth day (*daśāha*), there is impurity (*āśauca*) for ten days for both parents, and two days for others. If the death occurs before sunrise on the eleventh day (*ekādaśarātri*), there is three days of impurity for those other than the mother, father, and uterine brothers. If the death occurs after sunrise, there is ten days of impurity for the mother, father, uterine brothers, and brothers born of different wombs (*bhinnodarabhrātṛ*). Regarding birth, for those of the *kṣetraja* class and others, it is prescribed that there is one day of impurity for the parents, and only one day for their relatives (*jñāti*).

If [the husband] does not approach [his wife] during her fertile season, then the son born from the field (*kṣetraja*)—one produced by a brother-in-law (*devara*), or by a *sagotra*, or by another *sapiṇḍa*—is the "field-born" (*putra-kṣetraja*).

However, the son belonging to two lineages (*dvāmuṣyāyaṇa*) is distinguished by his connection to the biological father; he is distinct from one born from the field of another. Regarding the birth of the *kṣetraja*: (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with a discussion regarding the *kṣetraja* and the distinction of the *dvāmuṣyāyaṇa*.)

For the lord of the field and the lord of the seed, there is three-day impurity (*āśauca*). For those who are *jñāti* relatives within two *gotras*, there is one-day impurity. For those who are *jñāti* relatives beyond two *gotras*, there is no impurity upon his death. Regarding the parents, there is three days; for their [other] sons, it is immediate; and for them [the sons], there is three days at the death of the father. [Regarding] mother and father...

In the case of death—within three days for that son born of the field (kṣetraja). For Brāhmaṇas, the collection of the ancestors (pitṛsaṃgraha) should be performed by their sapindas; in their absence, it should be caused to be performed by those of the same lineage (sagotra), or even by a stranger.

For Śūdras, it is the same as that [rule regarding] the daughter’s son (dauhitra) or the sister’s son (bhāgineya). One who has only one son must not, under any effort, give away that son [in adoption]; nor should one take an only son [as an adopted son].

Manu said: "Even for one who is not the eldest son—[it is taught] that for those who have entered another *gotra*, the inheritance and the period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) cease; all this is declared regarding their own family. Viśvanādhi says: 'If one should adopt a son of another *gotra* as his own body-protector, then the lineage belongs only to the giver. If one makes an adoption from another *gotra*, he alone shall remain in that *gotra*; his sons, however, are established in the original *gotra*. Having taken a son..."

All such matters as the lineage (*gotra*) and so forth of the ancestors, which depend upon the specific state of their *saṃskāras* and life-stages (*āśrama*), [are determined by this]. Between father and son, up until the fifth generation and for nine years thereafter, [the property] may always be given or received by the twice-born (*dvija*).

1) The same applies to widows, non-widows, and likewise to those practicing celibacy (*brahmacārin*). In the Kali age, it should neither be accepted nor given; furthermore, the practice of appointing a brother-in-law (*devara*) is not permitted in the Kali age. (l. 2)

An appointed son (*dattaputra*) shall perform all rites for his father accompanied by his own father’s mother, and for the sake of his maternal grandfather, mother, and father; he shall do so for his eldest [biological] father until the fall of his body. (Manu 9.140) A man who has been duly appointed as a son shall perform the rites for his adopter; if the adopter is childless, he shall ultimately perform them for him as well. (Manu 9.141) But if, after a daughter has been designated as a son (*putrikā*), a son is subsequently born [to her], an equal division of the entire estate shall take place; in that case, the status of the eldest is not recognized. If a grandson (*dauhitraka*) exists after the adoption [of the daughter as a son]— [text breaks off].

Two persons shall share [the inheritance]. He stated that they should divide the portion equally—*jyeṣṭhāṃśaṃ na devayil* (the eldest’s special share is not to be given). Furthermore: "In the case of one of a different caste (*asavarṇa*), there is a fourth part;

in the case of one of the same caste (*savarṇa*), they are equal sharers. Bṛhaspati says: "Both the son and the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) cause the attainment of heaven," thus says the Smṛti. "In the paternal wealth, only one is declared the master; the appointed daughter is said to be equal to him, while the others are remembered as those who must be maintained. In the absence of a son, the daughter is entitled to the wealth...

The funeral rites for a Śūdra must be performed by a Śūdra alone. However, in certain circumstances due to the exigency of time, even a Brāhmaṇa may perform them for a Śūdra. For a Śūdra, there shall be a period of impurity lasting three nights until the seventh day; beyond that, it is merely bathing, as stated in the Vāsiṣṭha-bhāṣya. Manu says: "But [the impurity lasts] until the seventh generation has been united [in the rite]..."

When [the period of impurity] has ceased, the status of *samānodaka* (distant kinsmen) continues. After the fourteenth day, following the recollection of the lineage name (*gotra-nāma*), the lineage is said to be sevenfold. Regarding one who has died as a *sodaka*, there is three days of impurity; below that [status], it is immediate (*sadyas*). This is what is meant. For *jñātis* (agnates), [impurity lasts] until the third generation; they are called *jñātis*. For those *sapiṇḍas*, there is impurity for three nights (*śarātra*) on account of birth or marriage. Until that point, they are *samānodakas*; for them—

Three days—this applies to those above [the age of ten]. (21) *Paryantam*—for those of the same lineage (*sagotra*), there is one day of impurity (*āśauca*) for them. There is also the libation (*tarpaṇa*). (21) Above this, there is merely bathing; this is the same for both birth and death. On the day the menstrual flow is seen, from that day onwards, women remain impure for three days, until the end of the ten-day period...

Purity is prescribed as follows: for eighteen days after [the onset of menstruation], she becomes pure by bathing; beyond that, she remains impure for three nights. Any menstrual flow that occurs after a month has passed is declared to be "seasonal" (*kālaja*). (Verse 2) For women, purity begins from the third day after the appearance of the menses. Beyond that—up until the twelfth day—there is no impurity. Beyond the twelfth day—up until the eighteenth day—purity is attained through bathing every day. Beyond the eighteenth day—up until the twenty-first day—she is touchable, and beyond that, there is complete purification. Beyond one month... [text ends].
The period of menstruation. Manu says: "A woman who has bathed after her menses becomes pure on the fourth day; she may perform rites for the gods and ancestors once the flow has ceased. (l.

5) If she bathes from the first day of the *ṛtu* (menstrual period), she is fit only for [domestic] duties such as caring for children. From the second day onwards, she is fit for rites for the gods and ancestors. (l.

6) "If a woman's menses continue day after day due to illness, she is not impure because of that; it is recorded as a physiological disorder (*vaikārī*). As long as she maintains virtuous conduct, even while menstruating... (l. 7)

"Where it proceeds: when the menstrual flow has ceased, [the woman] is pure for domestic work and for sexual intercourse. On the first day she is called a *caṇḍālī*; on the second, a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmaghātinī*); on the third day... [she is called] a washerwoman (*rajakī*); on the fourth day she becomes pure. This means that even if there is a daily menstrual flow due to illness and the like, there is no impurity. That... (l. 2)

It has come down by way of modification: "When a *śrotriya* dies in one's own house, there is impurity for three days; if it is a non-*śrotriya*, for one day. But when a *śrotriya* dies in the village, there is impurity for one day; if it is a non-*śrotriya*, for a single day. When a *śrotriya* dies in the house—impurity for that house lasts for three days; if he is a non-*śrotriya*, for one day. "House-impurity [lasts] when a *śrotriya* dies in the village for one day; if it is a non-*śrotriya*, for a day. [This continues] until the cremation.

If the rites of offering rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water (*udaka*) are performed, it should be known that the period of impurity for the household lasts ten days; during that time, the deceased remains right there. If a *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas) dies in a village, [impurity lasts] one day; if an *aśrotriya*, there is no [such rule]. If the funeral rites (*pretakarma*) are performed in a single house, that house remains impure for ten days.
Those who carry a helpless (*anātha*) deceased Brāhmaṇa obtain the fruit of a sacrifice at every step; of this there is no doubt. "Helpless" means one who has no son, grandson, kinsmen, or relatives.
Mitra: Cattle, fields, wealth, and grain—[all these belong to] one [who is pure]. However, wherever the death of Śūdras and others may occur, the impurity for Śūdras affects only the house;
