impurity for the entire village does not exist. If the death of a Śūdra or others occurs within a village, there is no village-wide impurity; for only the house, there is one day of impurity. At the eighth [day], [the purification occurs].

In towns (*paṭṭana*) and indeed in royal cities (*rājadhāni*), one should perform worship in due order; no fault as previously mentioned exists there. In cities, towns, and so forth, there is no defect regarding the worship of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others. For those who are without a protector (*anātha*), for the uninitiated (*anupanīta*), and likewise for the deceased (*preta*), there is a threefold [impurity]. However, in the case of a corpse in a village or similar place, there is another fault. But in the event of the death of sages (*muni*), ascetics (*yati*), or those who have entered the bodies of others (*parakāyapraveśin*), no fault exists at the place where it occurs. And [this applies] to the one without a protector (*anātha*).

And regarding those not initiated [into Vedic study]: for women, ascetics (yatis), and lords of sages (munīśvaras), there is no impurity caused by a corpse within the village or the house upon their death. If a birth occurs in the house of a kinsman, but the father’s brother (pitṛdhātṛ) is present in that house, there is impurity for him; however, if the birth occurs in another house while he is away, there is no fault. If a woman who has recently given birth (odukrantāl) gives birth in the house of her own brother, the brother must observe impurity for one day. If the birth occurs in the house of her father, the mother and father must observe impurity for three days.

If a birth occurs in another's house—there is no period of impurity (*āśauca*) for anyone. Some say this is because the daughter was brought to her own home for the purpose of giving birth, because wealth was provided for that purpose, and because she is the bearer of the burden of childbirth. They further state that even when a daughter is born in another's house, the father’s family must perform the rites here [in their own home]. One should act according to local custom.
The father [performs the rites]: "The girl has been taken by the boy. Whatever is customary in such matters, he himself shall perform. (l.

4) Even if a girl is born in his own house, some maintain that there is a three-day period of impurity (*aśauca*). What need is there to mention if she is taken as a bride? At present, according to ancient custom (*pūrvācāra*), the verse says: "The bridegroom—when this bridegroom takes these three [persons], there is a three-day [impurity]; if it is a girl, there is one day"—this is how it is practiced. (l. 6)

[This is] the *Toḷappara-sammayittuvē*. In the case of a bird [death] occurring out of sight (*parokṣe*), one should not eat for two nights (*pakṣiṇī*); in this world, regarding the eating of food during a period of impurity (*premāna*), there is a ten-night period (*daśarātra*) for the death of daughters and parents, and for others, it is according to the specific [caste] sin (*aghama*). Upon the death of mother and father, for daughters, it is three days within the same fortnight (*samapakṣa*).

If one eats during the period of impurity (*sūtaka*) at the end of a *pakṣiṇī* [period] while the event is out of sight (*parokṣa*), there is ten nights of impurity (*daśarātram āśauca*), as well as the performance of a *kṛcchra* penance. This applies equally to mothers, fathers, and women. Regarding the question, "How can the purification for women other than the parents be accomplished? the venerable Manu has declared: "Purification shall occur in exactly three nights. This is the consensus of the sage Yama that for women, upon the death of mother or father, there are three days [of impurity]. In every respect, this three-day rule is established.

When a wife who has married another man dies during her period of impurity (*ṛtu*), it is prescribed for the husband that [impurity] lasts for three days. For two days on either side of that [period], and for three days when she is deceased, it is likewise for the husband. (l. 5) When a wife who has married another man... for both husbands, it is three days. In the event of the death of that husband, for that woman, according to the *Manda* [tradition], for both sets of kinsmen (*ubhayajñāti*) it is one day—[this] does not apply during a solar eclipse (*uparāga*). When a sister’s son (*bhāgineya*) or a daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) dies, three days are desired. Before the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), it is a "bird-day" (*pakṣiṇī*). (l. 7)

The sage Vasiṣṭha said: "Even for a woman, [the impurity lasts] until the *upanayana* ceremony; prior to the *upanayana*, it is for three days. After the *upanayana*, it is for one day for the mother-in-law, the father-in-law, the teacher, his wife, and his daughter. Or [it lasts] until the *vāsinaḥ* (resident students), the *antaśced* (if within the house), the *tryahaḥ* (three days), or the *mitrāhaḥ* (friend's day). [Regarding] the maternal uncle and the maternal aunt...

And [the same applies] to the teacher (*ācārya*) and his son... he who has appointed [them] as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) at his own sacrifice—for these disciples, for three days, there is mutual [impurity]. For the lineage of officiating priests, for three days, there is bathing only. If, prior to the death of the father-in-law or mother-in-law, the wife dies, the impurity (*āśauca*) shall be for one day. One should avoid the act of shaving (*kṣurikarma*). ... [In the case of] the death of a maternal uncle’s son, a maternal aunt, or a maternal uncle’s wife, there is impurity for one day. One should not shave—[in the case of] a maternal aunt (*mātṛṣvasṛ*).

Upon the death of a father or a brother, there is impurity for three days for their respective counterparts. Likewise upon the death of a maternal uncle, a maternal aunt, or a paternal grandmother—whether younger or older—there is impurity for three days. For a *taptakṛcchra*, three; for an *atikṛcchra*, two. As a substitute for a *cāndrāyaṇa*, one should perform eight gifts of cows. If cattle are not available, ten coins (*paṇa*) shall be paid as a fine for each cow.

One must perform [the rites] according to what has been prescribed. Even if wealth is lacking—one should not fail to perform the *kuṇapa-śrāddha* for one who is devoid of feet; even if there is no [proper] funeral procession (*gati*), one should perform the rite according to one's capacity. For others, it is always immediate. Upon the death of a student (*brahmacārin*) or a householder, [there is purification] for the relatives, even if they are situated in the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) or renunciant (*saṃnyāsa*) stages of life.

Upon the death of a *saṃnyāsin*—there is neither fire-ritual (*agni-saṃskāra*), nor the term "deceased" (*preta*), nor rice-balls and water, nor ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), and so forth. Regarding the procedure for a *saṃnyāsin*, it may be performed: during a *kṛcchra* penance, a festival for the gods, a *śrāddha*, a gift, a fire-oblation (*homa*), or at the conclusion of a sacrifice.

In the case of those engaged in [rites] that have already begun, there is immediate purification upon the onset of an impurity. This applies also to the commencement of the Kṛcchra penance, as well as to the commencement of a festival for the gods, a Śrāddha, a gift-giving, a Homa, a Japa, austerities, or a sacrifice—provided the intended purpose has not been abandoned. If the impurity of a relative or similar [impurity] occurs, there is merely immediate bathing.

Regarding birth and death impurities (*prasūti-sūtaka*): one may perform bathing, wearing white garments, and rites such as *karma* without hesitation. As for the commencement (*ārambha*): at the beginning of a sacrifice, it is the formal invitation (*varaṇa*);

for a vow (*vrata*) or a solemn resolve (*saṃkalpa*), it is the same; for a marriage and the like, it is the *nāndīmukha* rite; for a *śrāddha*, it is the preparation of the food; and for the first feeding of rice (*annaprāśana*) and other rites, it is the end of the [preparation].

When cooked food has been prepared, it must be given by others and consumed; there is no fault—this is the settled rule. Regarding the invitation for a sacrifice (*yajña*), the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for vows (*vrata*) and the like, the *nāndīmukha-śrāddha* for marriages and the like, and the commencement of cooking for a *śrāddha*. If the performer (*kartṛ*) incurs impurity due to a relative (*jñāti-aśauca*) during the middle of a *śrāddha*, there is no impurity until the conclusion (*udvāsa*). Others may take [the food] and even carry it away; for there is this scriptural statement: "Those who have sipped water after going to another house are all remembered as pure. (l. 7)

This concerns the subject of sipping water (*ācamana*) immediately after eating. Even one who is impure may perform the *tilatarpaṇa* (libation with sesame seeds and water) on the following day, provided it is done annually. At the time of a *śrāddha*, one should offer libations for as many ancestors as have been designated. The performer of the *śrāddha* may also perform the *tilatarpaṇa* on another day. [There is no restriction] regarding gifts, eclipses, sacrifices, or the birth of a son; [it is] unrestricted.

When a pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*) has been undertaken, when the *devapārāyaṇa* has been commenced, and when purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the *namaḥ-karma* have begun, [impurity] is considered immediate (*sadyas*). Also at the time of giving gifts (*dāna*), during an eclipse (*grahaṇa*), at a son’s festival (*putrotsava*), at the commencement of the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*), at the commencement of penance (*prāyaścitta*), on a pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*), at the commencement of the *upākarma*, at the commencement of a vow (*vṛta*), and at the commencement of various purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), if a *sūta* dies, there is merely a bath (*snānamātra*). [This applies] at the time of sacrifice (*yajña*), at weddings (*vivāha*), and at divine worship (*devayāga*).

In the case of an expiation (*niṣkṛti*), while the oblation is being offered into the fire, there is neither ritual impurity (*āśauca*) nor birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). There is no impurity during a sacrifice, a wedding, a festival for a deity, or an act of atonement (*prāyaścitta*). Even during a period of impurity, one may observe the vow of Ekādaśī; however, other vows cannot be observed. Slaves, male and female, kings, ministers, artisans, craftsmen, and physicians—[these too are exempt]. (Note: *Sūtakam* refers to the state of impurity following a birth; *āśaucam* is the general term for ritual impurity resulting from death or birth.)

In their respective duties, they are always pure or impure; this does not apply to other activities. One should not perform acts such as salutation (*vandanā*) while assuming the form of a deity. For those in a state of ritual impurity (*āśauca*), entering a temple and performing salutations and the like are forbidden. However, for those who have passed a month [of mourning], they may perform their own respective duties. It is traditionally taught that elsewhere, even a son born from a *sūtā* woman is considered pure in mind.

That which has been eaten by the Blessed One is commended for rites pertaining to the ancestors, the gods, and so forth. The remains of what was eaten by the Blessed One may not be consumed by one who is far away, nor by a woman in childbirth, nor by one who has touched a corpse, nor by one who is in a state of ritual impurity (*āśauca*). If the wind blows for three nights, there is [impurity] for three days; if it blows for ten nights, there is [impurity] for ten days. And until the end of death... [impurity lasts] for ten days. If the removal of the corpse is performed by one who is not a relative (*anindriya*), there is immediate purification, which yields great fruit. The removal of a corpse for the sake of a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) by non-kin (*ajñāti*) results in double the sin for those who are kin. Regarding those of different castes (*vijāti*), Gautama states here that for one of the same caste (*sajāti*), the impurity is as prescribed for that caste. Even if one performs the decoration of the corpse, carries it out, burns it, or goes to another village, there is impurity for that day; however, within that same village... [there is no impurity].
If one resides in that house for one day, eats there for three days, and stays for ten days, it constitutes the impurity of an *anātha-yatīśvara* (a masterless ascetic).

For him, there is no ritual bathing (*snāna*); merely bathing suffices. If he carries [the corpse] or burns it, he incurs the fruit of a sacrifice (*yajñaphala*). There is no impurity (*āśauca*) [for his own kin]. If he is a relative, however, the double period of impurity applies.

If a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya carries [the corpse], there is an impurity of thirty-two days. If a Vaiśya carries it, there is an impurity of forty days. If a Śūdra carries it, [there is the full period of impurity].

There is impurity for two months. When following a corpse, one is not unfit for ritual acts on that day [if it is] the following of a corpse that is not a relative. Even by performing the following of a non-relative's corpse... (p.37a, l.1)...

even by having performed it, for him—for that [day] alone—the rites for the gods and ancestors and so forth must be avoided. But regarding the funeral rites for the deceased, one who was previously defiled by impurity becomes pure at that very moment. (l.2)

Regarding impurity due to death (*satyāśauca*): one does not become impure for ten days on account of a fall [from a cliff] or similar accidents. However, if a *brahmacārin* performs the *saṃskāra* rites for his mother, father, or others, he must bathe at the conclusion of each daily ritual; otherwise, there is no impurity. If one eats in a house where a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) exists, the impurity lasts for ten days. (L. 4) Those of the twice-born (*dvijāti*) castes who follow the corpse of a member of their own caste are purified by bathing, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter (*ājya*), along with the observance of restraints such as fasting. For those who follow the corpse of a *śūdra*, purification takes three days. (L. 5)
For a twice-born person following the corpse of another twice-born person, there is impurity for three days. For one following the corpse of a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya, there is impurity for two days.

A Śūdra who follows the corpse of a twice-born person becomes pure by bathing at the end of the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). If a Śūdra follows the corpse of a Brāhmaṇa, there is impurity for three days. If he follows the corpse of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, there is impurity for two days. Furthermore, at the conclusion of the *sūtaka*, if he bathes in a river and performs the recitation (*japa*) of the Gāyatrī mantra sixty thousand times, he becomes pure. If a Śūdra follows the corpse of a twice-born person, he becomes pure by bathing. [The text is incomplete here.]
